title: Hidden Moisture Damage Behind Your Siding
description: Paint blistering at siding laps often means the wall behind is already wet. Learn the warning signs, where water gets in, and how the damage is repaired.
excerpt: When paint blisters at siding laps, the sheathing behind is often already wet. Warning signs, entry points, and how repairs are done.
h1: Hidden Moisture Damage Behind Your Siding
heroIntro: Siding is a rain screen, not a waterproof shell. Some water always gets behind it. Problems start when that water cannot get back out, and by the time paint bubbles on the face, the damage underneath has often been building for a while.

questions: How do you know if there is water damage behind siding?
What causes paint to blister on siding?
Can pressure washing cause water damage behind siding?

body: Every wall has weak points where different materials meet. In North Central Florida, with wind-driven summer rain and long humid stretches, those details get tested constantly. The most common entry points:
bullets: Missing or failed kickout flashing where a roof edge meets a wall, which sends roof runoff straight into the wall.
Window and door heads without proper flashing, and perimeter caulk that has cracked or pulled away.
Unsealed penetrations: hose bibs, dryer vents, light fixtures, cable and AC lines.
Siding installed too close to the ground, a roof, or a deck, so it wicks water up into the cut ends.
Boards that were never back-primed or end-sealed at install, which absorb water from behind.
Pressure washing aimed upward under the laps.

body: You cannot see the sheathing, but the face of the wall leaves clues. Walk the house slowly and look for:
bullets: Paint blisters or peeling concentrated at the bottom edges of laps or below windows
Swollen, cupped, or split board ends, especially near butt joints
Rust streaks running from nail heads
Dark staining or mildew lines that follow a pattern, such as a diagonal under a roofline
Soft, punky trim at the base of corner boards and door casings
Siding that moves or sounds hollow when pressed
Caulk joints that have split or shrunk away

body: Water that has made it through the sheathing often shows up indoors: stained or swelling baseboards on exterior walls, bubbling interior paint near windows, a musty smell in one room, or flooring that is cupping along an outside wall. If you see these, our guide to bubbling paint on drywall helps you tell a surface issue from a wall-cavity leak.

sections.h2: Diagnosing what is behind the wall
body: A pin moisture meter on the siding and trim gives readings you can compare across the house: dry areas versus suspect ones. An awl or small screwdriver tells you if wood is soft. The definitive step is to open the area: remove a few courses of siding below the suspect spot and look at the housewrap and sheathing directly. Professionals sometimes use thermal cameras to spot cool, wet areas, but opening the wall is still how you confirm the extent. Take photos as you go; they help any contractor or insurer understand what was found and what was replaced.

Work from the bottom of the stain pattern up. Water runs down inside the wall, so the visible damage is often below the actual entry point, and fixing only where it shows will leave the leak in place.

bullets: Find and correct the water source: add kickout flashing, flash window heads, seal penetrations, or fix grade and clearance.
Remove damaged siding, trim, and any wet or rotted sheathing.
Let the cavity dry, and treat any mold growth appropriately.
Replace sheathing and repair or patch the weather-resistive barrier, lapping it correctly so water sheds outward.
Back-prime and end-seal every new board before installing it, and keep proper clearances from grade and roofing.
Re-caulk joints that should be sealed, leave drainage paths open, prime, and paint with two coats of quality exterior acrylic.
body: The order below matters, and the first step is the one most often skipped. Carpentry, flashing, and sheathing work may call for a qualified siding contractor or general contractor alongside the painters.

bullets: Wood lap siding: end grain at butt joints and the bottom edge of each board soak up water first; unprimed backs cup and split.
Fiber cement: very rot-resistant itself, but cut edges that were not sealed can swell, and the wood framing and sheathing behind it can still rot if water gets in.
Hardboard and composite siding from older builds: swells and softens at the bottom edges and around nails when the paint film is broken.
T1-11 and plywood panel siding: delaminates at the bottom edge and at horizontal joints without proper Z-flashing.
Vinyl: does not rot, but it is designed to let some water behind it, so flashing and housewrap quality decide whether the wall stays dry.
body: Knowing which type you have tells you where to look first. Paint is the first line of defense on wood-based products, so keeping the film intact, especially on bottom edges and around nails, is part of moisture control. On every type, the details around windows, doors, and roof lines matter more than the open wall.

sections.h2: Why painting over it does not help
body: A fresh coat of paint over wet wood traps moisture in, and the blisters return, often bigger. Worse, it hides the problem from the next inspection. This is one reason a careful exterior painter probes and photographs suspect areas before quoting, and why rot and fascia replacement is part of proper prep rather than an afterthought. For more on prep that lasts, read our exterior painting secrets.

Check caulk joints and flashing every spring before the rainy season. Make sure gutters and downspouts carry water well away from the walls. Keep mulch and soil several inches below the bottom of the siding, and trim shrubs back so walls can dry. When washing the house, aim the spray level or downward and use low pressure; never spray up under the laps. Touch up paint on bottom edges and nail heads as soon as you see it break, since that is where wood-based siding starts drinking water. If you are unsure whether a wall is wet, ask for a free estimate; Precision Paint Experts crew leads take moisture readings where needed during the walkthrough, and rot repair is part of our exterior painting prep.

faqs.q: How can I tell if there is water damage behind my siding?
faqs.a: Look for blistering paint at lap edges, swollen board ends, rust streaks from nails, soft trim, and stained baseboards inside. A moisture meter and opening a small section confirm it.

faqs.q: Can pressure washing cause damage behind siding?
faqs.a: Yes, if water is sprayed upward under laps or at high pressure. Use a low-pressure soft wash and keep the spray angled level or downward.
A small angled flashing at the bottom of a roof edge where it meets a wall. It directs roof runoff away from the siding. When it is missing, water often pours into the wall.

faqs.q: Can I just repaint over blistered siding?
faqs.a: Not until the moisture source is fixed and the wood is dry and sound. Paint over wet or rotted wood will blister again and hides the damage.
